details:
**Knight, Death and the Devil**
One of Dürer's three "Master Engravings," made in 1513. An armored knight rides calmly through a dark, rocky forest, followed by his dog. He ignores Death, a decaying figure with snakes in his crown who rides a pale horse and holds up an hourglass, and a goat-headed, pig-snouted Devil carrying a pronged staff. A lizard scurries on the ground below.

**Melencolia I**
A 1514 Master Engraving of a brooding, laurel-wreathed winged figure who sits holding a compass among unused tools, with a sleeping dog, a cherub, a sphere, and a large irregular polyhedron now called "Dürer's solid." An hourglass, a balance, a bell, and a 4-by-4 magic square hang on the wall behind her, and the bottom row of the square reads 1514. The title is shown on a banner held by a bat-like creature flying in front of a rainbow.

**St. Jerome in His Study**
The third Master Engraving, made in 1514. St. Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible, writes at a desk in a sunlit room. A lion and a sleeping dog lie in the foreground, a gourd hangs from the ceiling, and a skull sits on the windowsill.

**Rhinoceros**
Dürer's 1515 woodcut of an Indian rhinoceros that was sent to Lisbon, the first live rhinoceros in Europe since Roman times. Dürer never saw the animal and worked from a written description and sketch sent by Valentim Fernandes. He gave it inaccurate armor-like plates with rivets, scales, and a small extra horn on its back, yet for centuries Europeans believed rhinos looked like this.

**The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse**
The most famous woodcut from Dürer's 1498 Apocalypse series, which illustrates the Book of Revelation. Four riders, often identified as Conquest, War, Famine (holding a set of scales), and Death on a pale horse, trample people as they charge. Another print in the series shows St. John eating a book given to him by an angel.

**Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight (1500)**
Dürer's 1500 self-portrait faces the viewer head-on with symmetrical features and long curly hair, like traditional images of Christ as Salvator Mundi. He holds the fur collar of his coat. The inscription says he painted himself "with indelible colors at the age of 28 years."

**Young Hare and Great Piece of Turf**
Two pioneering, extremely realistic watercolor nature studies. Young Hare (1502) shows a hare with every hair carefully painted, and Great Piece of Turf (1503) shows a tangled clump of wild grasses and weeds. His Wing of a Blue Roller is a similar study.

**Praying Hands**
A famous drawing of two hands pressed together in prayer, done on blue-tinted paper as a study for an altarpiece. It appears on the cover of Drake's mixtape If You're Reading This It's Too Late.

**The Feast of the Rose Garlands**
An altarpiece Dürer painted in Venice in 1506 for German merchants there, influenced by Giovanni Bellini. The Virgin Mary, the Christ Child, and St. Dominic hand out garlands of roses to kneeling figures, including the pope and the Holy Roman Emperor.

**The Martyrdom of the Ten Thousand**
A painting of the legendary massacre of ten thousand Christians on Mount Ararat by the forces of the Persian king Shapur I, with many people crucified and killed in the foreground. Dürer painted himself and a friend dressed in black standing among the carnage.

**The Four Apostles**
Dürer's 1526 pair of tall panels for the city of Nuremberg. The left panel shows St. John the Evangelist in red reading a book while St. Peter looks on. The right panel shows St. Paul with St. Mark behind him.

**AD monogram**
Dürer's famous signature, a large "A" with a small "D" set beneath its crossbar. It often appears on a tablet or plaque in his prints along with the date. When Marcantonio Raimondi copied his prints, signature included, Dürer took him to court, an early case over artistic copyright.

**Self-Portrait with Thistle and Michael Wolgemut**
Dürer trained in Nuremberg under the painter and woodcut designer Michael Wolgemut. Soon after his apprenticeship, in 1493, he painted his first self-portrait, showing himself in a red cap and holding a thistle, possibly as an engagement picture.

**Emperor Maximilian I and The Triumphal Arch**
The Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I was Dürer's patron. For him Dürer designed The Triumphal Arch, a giant print made from many woodblocks, and the Large Triumphal Carriage, which shows the emperor in a chariot pulled by six pairs of horses. Frederick the Wise of Saxony was another patron.

**Four Books on Human Proportion**
Dürer's theoretical treatise on measuring and drawing the human body, published in 1528, the year he died. He also wrote a treatise on geometry and measurement, part of his effort to bring Italian Renaissance theory to Germany.
